title: Pythagoras
orientation: This chapter presents Pythagoras as both a religious prophet, founder of an ascetic order teaching the transmigration of souls, and the founder of demonstrative mathematics, arguing that these two sides -- described by Russell as 'a combination of Einstein and Mrs. Eddy' -- were not separate but intimately fused. It matters because Russell traces the entire subsequent European tradition of blending mathematics, mysticism, and theology (through Plato, Augustine, Aquinas, Descartes, Spinoza, and Kant) back to this fusion.
historical_background: Pythagoras was born on Samos, ruled during his lifetime by the tyrant Polycrates (a rich, unscrupulous pirate-ruler eventually crucified by the Persian satrap at Sardes), and left the island because he disliked Polycrates' government, settling instead at Croton in southern Italy. Croton and the neighboring city of Sybaris were among the richest Greek cities of Italy, living by importing Ionian goods for local use and re-export to Gaul and Spain; Croton destroyed Sybaris in 510 B.C. shortly after Pythagoras's arrival. Pythagoras founded an influential religious-political society at Croton, but was eventually driven out and died at Metapontion.
philosophical_problems: What is the relationship between mathematical/intellectual contemplation and religious salvation or purification of the soul?
Can 'all things' really be explained as, or reduced to, numbers?
Does the discovery of incommensurable magnitudes refute the idea that reality is fundamentally numerical?
Is thought (the intelligible, exact world of mathematics) more real or trustworthy than sense-perception (the changing physical world)?

philosophers_discussed.name: Pythagoras
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Central figure: founder of a religious order teaching transmigration of souls and ascetic taboos, and, more importantly for later philosophy, founder of demonstrative mathematics and the doctrine that 'all things are numbers', fusing intellectual contemplation with religious salvation.

schools_discussed: Orphism (as a precursor reformed by Pythagoras)

core_concepts.name: 'All things are numbers' and the mathematization of reality
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Pythagoras thought of numbers as shapes (like dots on dice), discovered that musical harmony depends on numerical ratios, and concluded that the physical and aesthetic world could ultimately be understood through arithmetic and geometric relationships.
core_concepts.precise_definition: The Pythagorean doctrine that the fundamental nature of things is number: numbers were conceived as shapes built from units ('pebbles'), musical intervals were shown to correspond to simple numerical ratios, and the world was pictured as atomic bodies built from units arranged in geometric patterns.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: Russell calls this the beginning of a philosophical tradition, running through Plato and down to Kant, in which mathematical, exact, timeless knowledge is taken as a model for -- and evidence of the superiority of -- a supersensible intelligible world over the changing world of the senses.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Attributed to Pythagoras's discovery of the numerical basis of musical intervals and of figurate numbers (square, oblong, triangular, pyramidal).
examples: The terms 'harmonic mean' and 'harmonic progression', surviving from Pythagoras's musical discoveries
'Square' and 'cube' numbers, and figurate (triangular, pyramidal) numbers represented as arrangements of pebbles
objections: The discovery of incommensurable magnitudes (e.g. the diagonal of a unit square), which showed that not all lengths stand in whole-number ratios to one another, appeared to disprove the doctrine that everything reduces to (whole) numbers
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Directly inspires Plato's doctrine that 'God is a geometer' and the broader idea of an eternal, intelligible world revealed to intellect rather than sense; Russell traces this line down through Augustine, Aquinas, Descartes, Spinoza, and Kant.
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: For Pythagoras, mathematical 'theory' (intellectual contemplation) was itself a religious act, the highest form of the purification that frees the soul from the 'wheel of birth'.

core_concepts.name: Transmigration of souls and the Pythagorean religious order
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Pythagoras founded a religious brotherhood, admitting men and women equally and holding property in common, that believed souls are reborn repeatedly in different bodies (even animal bodies) and can be purified over many lifetimes; the order followed a long list of taboo-like rules, such as abstaining from beans.
core_concepts.precise_definition: The Pythagorean doctrine, inherited and reformed from Orphism, that the soul is immortal and is reincarnated in a cycle of rebirths ('nothing being absolutely new'), and that all living things, being kindred, should be treated accordingly; embodied in an ascetic religious community governed by numerous ritual taboos.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: Establishes Pythagoras, in Russell's account (following Cornford), as an 'offshoot' of the mystical, Orphic current of Greek religion rather than the scientific/Ionian one, even though his mathematics is treated as scientifically serious.
core_concepts.historical_origin: A reform of Orphism, itself a reform of the worship of Dionysus/Bacchus (as described in Chapter I).
examples: The rule to abstain from beans
The rule not to touch a white cock or step over a crossbar
Pythagoras allegedly recognizing the soul of a dead friend in a beaten dog's cry (per Xenophanes' mockery)
objections: Xenophanes' satirical anecdote mocking the doctrine of transmigration
competing_positions: The rationalist, non-mystical Ionian tradition of the Milesians
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Feminism within the order (claimed equality of the sexes) is said by Russell to anticipate, and go on to influence, Plato's proposal of political equality for women.
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: The Pythagorean order at times acquired direct political control of Croton, establishing what Russell calls 'a rule of the saints', though it was eventually overthrown.

core_concepts.name: The contemplative ideal and the origin of 'theory'
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Pythagoras taught that the best kind of life is neither buying and selling nor competing, but simply looking on -- disinterested contemplation, especially of mathematical truths -- which he considered the highest form of purification of the soul.
core_concepts.precise_definition: An ethical and metaphysical doctrine, summarized by Russell via Burnet's account of the 'three kinds of men' at the Olympic Games, holding that disinterested intellectual contemplation ('theoria') is the greatest purification and the truest philosophy, releasing the soul from the 'wheel of birth'.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: This ideal gave the pursuit of pure (non-applied) mathematics unprecedented prestige, and, in Russell's view, is the historical source of the enduring Western association between disinterested truth, the contemplative life, and philosophical/theological dignity.
core_concepts.historical_origin: A specifically Pythagorean transformation of the originally Orphic, ecstatic sense of 'theoria' into an intellectual, mathematical sense.
examples: Burnet's analogy of three types of visitors to the Olympic Games: those who buy and sell, those who compete, and those who simply look on (the highest)
competing_positions: Modern, industrial/pragmatist values that esteem the active competitor (the 'player') over the contemplative spectator
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Russell connects this directly to the long philosophical prestige of the 'gentleman'/contemplative ideal, which depended historically on a society resting on slave labor.
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Directly religious: contemplation is presented as a path to salvation from the cycle of rebirth.

core_concepts.name: The discovery of incommensurable magnitudes
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Pythagoras's own theorem about right-angled triangles led to the discovery that the diagonal of a square cannot be measured exactly by any whole-number ratio relative to its side -- a result that seemed to undermine Pythagoras's belief that everything could be understood through (whole) numbers.
core_concepts.precise_definition: The proof, using the Pythagorean theorem, that for a right isosceles triangle with legs of length 1, the hypotenuse's length cannot be expressed as a ratio m/n of integers, since assuming so leads to a contradiction (m and n would each have to be both odd and even).
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: This discovery forced Greek mathematicians (culminating in Euclid) to develop geometry independently of arithmetic, shaping the entire subsequent Euclidean tradition and, through it, later philosophy's model of self-evident axioms and deduction (e.g. the U.S. Declaration of Independence's 'self-evident' truths, modeled on Euclid).
core_concepts.historical_origin: A consequence of the Pythagorean theorem, discovered by Pythagoras or his immediate disciples.
core_concepts.associated_philosopher: Pythagoras (theorem); later formalized in Euclid, Book X
examples: The proof that no fraction m/n measures the hypotenuse of a unit right isosceles triangle
Euclid's geometric (rather than algebraic) proofs of results like (a+b)^2 = a^2 + 2ab + b^2, necessitated by the problem of incommensurables
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Shaped the axiomatic-deductive form of Euclid's Elements, which in turn influenced Plato, Kant, Newton's Principia, and even the rhetoric of the Declaration of Independence and Enlightenment natural-rights theory.

arguments.title: Proof of the incommensurability of the diagonal and side of a square
arguments.philosopher: Pythagoras (attributed; proof as reconstructed by Russell after Euclid)
premises: Suppose the hypotenuse of a unit right isosceles triangle has length m/n in lowest terms (so not both m and n are even).
By the Pythagorean theorem, m^2/n^2 = 2, so m^2 = 2n^2, meaning m^2 (and therefore m) is even.
If m is even, say m = 2p, then 4p^2 = 2n^2, so n^2 = 2p^2, meaning n^2 (and therefore n) is even too.
But m and n cannot both be even, since the fraction was assumed to be in lowest terms.
arguments.conclusion: No fraction m/n can measure the hypotenuse; the diagonal and the side of a square are incommensurable.
arguments.explanation: Russell walks through this proof (substantially Euclid's, Book X) in detail as the historically pivotal argument that shattered the naive Pythagorean hope of reducing all geometric relations to whole-number ratios.
implications: Forced the separation of geometry from arithmetic in Greek mathematics, culminating in Euclid's geometric treatment of what we would now handle algebraically.
Undermined, without destroying, the broader Pythagorean metaphysical program of explaining reality through number.

arguments.title: The three kinds of men at the Olympic Games (the case for the contemplative life)
premises: At the Olympic Games there are three kinds of people: those who come to buy and sell, those who compete, and those who simply look on.
Of these, the disinterested spectator, seeking neither profit nor victory, occupies the highest, most honorable position.
Philosophy, understood as disinterested contemplation (paradigmatically of mathematical truths), is the intellectual analogue of this highest kind of spectatorship.
arguments.conclusion: Disinterested science/contemplation is the greatest purification, and the true philosopher is the one most fully released from 'the wheel of birth'.
arguments.explanation: Russell presents this as the ethical bridge connecting Pythagoras's mysticism to his mathematics: mathematics is valued not merely for its results but as itself a religious, purifying activity.
implications: Explains the enduring prestige of 'pure' (non-applied) knowledge and the contemplative ideal in Western philosophy and theology.
Presupposes and reflects a social order (the 'gentleman' living on slave or others' labor) that Russell explicitly flags as historically contingent.

key_distinctions: Pythagoras as religious prophet versus Pythagoras as mathematician (two aspects Russell insists were not separate for him or his followers)
Thought/intellect (associated with exact, eternal mathematical truth) versus sense-perception (associated with the changing, imperfect physical world)
The contemplative spectator versus the competitor or trader, as rival models of the best kind of life
connections_to_earlier_philosophers: Pythagoras is presented as a reformer of Orphism (itself traced in Chapter I to the cult of Dionysus/Bacchus), and as influenced by Anaximenes' Milesian speculation (Chapter II); Cornford is quoted describing Parmenides as 'an offshoot of Pythagoreanism'.
connections_to_later_philosophers: Russell states directly that 'what appears as Platonism is, when analysed, found to be in essence Pythagoreanism', crediting Pythagoras with the whole conception of an eternal, intelligible world underlying Plato's philosophy, and, through Plato, Christian theology (e.g. proofs of God and immortality) and the later mathematical-theological tradition running through Augustine, Aquinas, Descartes, Spinoza, and Kant.
political_social_context: The Pythagorean society at Croton held property in common, admitted women on equal terms with men, and at times gained direct political control of the city (a 'rule of the saints') before being overthrown; Russell also situates the contemplative ideal within a social order resting on slave labor, since the 'gentleman' free to contemplate depended on others' labor.
religion_science_culture_context: The chapter treats mathematics as originally and essentially bound up with religion for Pythagoras, and identifies this fusion as the specific European contribution -- as against the 'more straightforward mysticism of Asia' -- of an intellectualized theology combining moral aspiration with logical admiration of the timeless.
russell_presentation: Russell presents Pythagoras as one of the most historically influential and psychologically strange figures in the book, memorably described as 'a combination of Einstein and Mrs. Eddy'. He treats the religious/ascetic side (transmigration, taboo rules, semi-divine self-conception) and the mathematical side (the theorem, figurate numbers, the discovery of incommensurables) as genuinely fused rather than coincidentally combined, arguing that Pythagoras's ethic of disinterested contemplation is precisely what connects mysticism to mathematics. Russell credits Pythagoras with founding the entire subsequent tradition, culminating in Plato and running to Kant, in which mathematical certainty is taken to reveal a superior, eternal, intelligible world behind the deceptive world of the senses -- a tradition he regards as 'both profound and unfortunate' in its influence on philosophy. He closes by asserting Platonism is 'in essence Pythagoreanism' and crediting Pythagoras with making possible later Christian and philosophical arguments for God and immortality.
critical_context: Historiographical note: Russell relies substantially on Cornford's interpretive framework (from 'From Religion to Philosophy'), which reads Pythagoreanism as continuous with Orphic mysticism; this is a specific early-20th-century scholarly thesis rather than an uncontested fact, and Russell elsewhere (Chapter III itself, and again regarding Cornford in Chapter I) expresses some reservations about trusting Cornford's interpretations fully. Modern scholarship remains divided on how much of the mathematics attributed to 'Pythagoras' is his personally versus the collective, anonymous work of later Pythagoreans.
key_takeaways: Pythagoras founded both an ascetic religious order teaching transmigration of souls and the tradition of demonstrative, deductive mathematics -- and, for Russell, these two sides were genuinely fused, not merely coincidental.
The Pythagorean order held property in common, admitted women equally, and briefly gained direct political power at Croton before being overthrown.
Pythagoras's doctrine 'all things are numbers' grew out of his discovery of numerical ratios underlying musical harmony and his conception of numbers as geometric shapes built from units.

The Pythagorean theorem led to the discovery of incommensurable magnitudes (e.g. the diagonal of a unit square), which threatened the doctrine that reality reduces to whole numbers and forced Greek mathematics to separate geometry from arithmetic.
Pythagoras's ethic of disinterested contemplation as the highest, most purifying way of life gave mathematics unprecedented religious and philosophical prestige.
Russell traces the entire subsequent European fusion of mathematics and theology -- through Plato, Augustine, Aquinas, Descartes, Spinoza, and Kant -- back to Pythagoras.
study_notes:
The key interpretive move to hold onto in this chapter is Russell's insistence that Pythagoras's mysticism and his mathematics are not two separate achievements accidentally combined in one biography, but a single intellectual attitude: mathematical contemplation just is, for Pythagoras, a religious practice, the purest available form of the soul's purification. Once you see this, several otherwise odd features of later philosophy make more sense -- for instance, why Plato treats mathematical objects as more 'real' than sensible ones, or why medieval and early modern philosophers (Augustine, Aquinas, Descartes, Spinoza) so often reach for geometric or quasi-geometric method when discussing God.

Pay close attention also to the incommensurability proof: it is worth working through step by step, both because it is a genuine, historically important piece of mathematics presented in accessible form, and because Russell uses it to make a general point about how philosophically important discoveries can refute a theory's letter (that everything is expressible in whole numbers) without destroying its spirit (a broader trust in the special authority of mathematical, as opposed to sensory, knowledge) -- a pattern of 'partial refutation' Russell will return to elsewhere in the book.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: The belief that after death, a soul is reborn in a new body -- possibly even an animal's -- and this cycle repeats many times.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: The Pythagorean (and Orphic) doctrine that the soul is immortal and passes through successive incarnations, its progress toward purification or its degree of pollution determining the nature of each subsequent embodiment.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: Two lengths (like the side and diagonal of a square) that cannot both be measured exactly by whole-number multiples of some common unit.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: Magnitudes between which there exists no ratio of integers m:n such that m times one equals n times the other; discovered via the Pythagorean theorem applied to the unit right isosceles triangle, and later handled rigorously in Euclid, Book X.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: The Greek root of our word 'theory', originally meaning passionate, quasi-religious contemplation, later redirected by Pythagoras toward intellectual and mathematical contemplation.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: Originally an Orphic term for ecstatic, sympathetic identification with a suffering god; transformed by Pythagoras into disinterested intellectual contemplation, understood as the highest form of purification and the origin of the modern sense of 'theory'.

questions.prompt: In what two respects, according to Russell, was Pythagoras 'intellectually one of the most important men that ever lived'?
questions.answer: As the founder of demonstrative, deductive mathematics, and as the source of a peculiar mysticism (an ascetic religious order teaching transmigration of souls) that became intimately connected with that mathematics.
questions.explanation: Russell insists these two sides were fused, not separate, in Pythagoras and his followers.

questions.prompt: Reconstruct the proof that the hypotenuse of a unit right isosceles triangle cannot be measured by a whole-number ratio.
questions.answer: Assume the hypotenuse equals m/n in lowest terms. By the Pythagorean theorem, m^2/n^2 = 2, so m^2 = 2n^2, making m even. If m = 2p, then n^2 = 2p^2, making n even too -- contradicting the assumption that m/n was in lowest terms (not both even). Therefore no such fraction exists.
questions.explanation: This is the historically pivotal discovery of incommensurability, substantially the proof given in Euclid, Book X.

questions.prompt: What example does Burnet's account of the Pythagorean ethic use to explain why 'disinterested science' is the highest form of purification?
questions.answer: The analogy of three kinds of people who attend the Olympic Games: those who come to buy and sell (lowest), those who compete, and those who come simply to look on (highest) -- the philosopher-contemplative corresponds to this highest, disinterested spectator.
questions.explanation: This links Pythagoras's religious ethic directly to his valorization of pure, contemplative mathematics.

questions.prompt: Contrast the social rules and organization of the Pythagorean order with those of a typical Greek philosophical school of the period, as Russell describes them.
questions.answer: The Pythagorean order was a genuine religious community: it admitted men and women on equal terms, held property in common, deemed scientific discoveries collectively owed to Pythagoras even after his death, and enforced numerous taboo-like rules (e.g. abstaining from beans); it also at times directly seized political power in Croton.
questions.explanation: This distinguishes Pythagoras's school from a purely intellectual or purely political institution, reflecting its Orphic religious roots.

questions.prompt: Which later Greek philosopher does Cornford (as quoted by Russell) call 'an offshoot of Pythagoreanism' and 'the discoverer of logic'?
questions.explanation: This connects Pythagoras forward to the Eleatic school treated in the next two chapters.

questions.prompt: According to Russell, what did the discovery of incommensurable magnitudes force Greek mathematicians (culminating in Euclid) to do?
questions.answer: To develop geometry independently of arithmetic, proving results we would now handle algebraically (such as (a+b)^2 = a^2+2ab+b^2) by purely geometric means.
questions.explanation: This shaped the axiomatic-deductive form of Euclid's Elements, later influential on Descartes, Newton, and even Enlightenment political rhetoric.

flashcards.back: 'A combination of Einstein and Mrs. Eddy.'

flashcards.front: What did Pythagoras discover about musical intervals?
flashcards.back: That they correspond to simple numerical ratios, giving rise to terms like 'harmonic mean' and 'harmonic progression'.

flashcards.front: What foods or actions did Pythagorean taboo rules forbid?
flashcards.back: Among others: eating beans, touching a white cock, stepping over a crossbar, and picking up what has fallen.

flashcards.front: What famous theorem is attributed to Pythagoras or his immediate disciples?
flashcards.back: The Pythagorean theorem: in a right triangle, the sum of the squares on the two legs equals the square on the hypotenuse.

flashcards.front: What mathematical discovery threatened the doctrine 'all things are numbers'?
flashcards.back: The discovery of incommensurable magnitudes, e.g. that the diagonal and side of a square share no common whole-number ratio.

flashcards.front: In Burnet's Olympic Games analogy, which of the three types of visitor represents the true philosopher?
flashcards.back: The disinterested spectator who comes simply to look on, ranked above traders and competitors.

flashcards.front: What social features distinguished the Pythagorean order from ordinary Greek society?
flashcards.back: Common property, admission of women on equal terms with men, and collective (not individual) credit for discoveries.

flashcards.front: Which later philosopher does Russell say is, 'when analysed', essentially Pythagoreanism?
flashcards.back: Plato -- Russell says 'what appears as Platonism is, when analysed, found to be in essence Pythagoreanism.'

flashcards.back: Figurate numbers -- e.g. square numbers, oblong numbers, triangular numbers, and pyramidal numbers.

quiz.prompt: In what southern Italian city did Pythagoras found his religious and philosophical society?
quiz.explanation: Pythagoras settled at Croton after leaving Samos and founded his order of disciples there.
quiz.related_concept: Transmigration of souls and the Pythagorean religious order

quiz.prompt: What famous mathematical result is attributed to Pythagoras or his immediate disciples?
options: The theorem that the earth is round
The theorem about right-angled triangles (sum of squares on the two sides equals the square on the hypotenuse)
quiz.explanation: Russell describes this as 'the greatest discovery of Pythagoras, or of his immediate disciples.'

quiz.prompt: What mathematical discovery appeared to disprove Pythagoras's doctrine that 'all things are numbers'?
options: Incommensurable magnitudes (e.g. the diagonal of a unit square)
quiz.explanation: The proof that the hypotenuse of a unit right isosceles triangle cannot be expressed as a whole-number ratio undermined the idea that all magnitudes reduce to whole numbers.
quiz.related_concept: 'All things are numbers' and the mathematization of reality

quiz.prompt: The Pythagorean order admitted only men and excluded women from membership.
quiz.explanation: Russell states that men and women were admitted to the Pythagorean society on equal terms.
quiz.related_concept: Transmigration of souls and the Pythagorean religious order

quiz.prompt: In Burnet's analogy (quoted by Russell) of the three kinds of visitors to the Olympic Games, which type represents the highest, most philosophical way of life?
options: Those who come to buy and sell
Those who come simply to look on
quiz.explanation: The disinterested spectator, seeking neither profit nor victory, represents the contemplative ideal Pythagoras associated with true philosophy.
quiz.related_concept: The contemplative ideal and the origin of 'theory'

quiz.prompt: According to Russell, what is 'in essence' Pythagoreanism when properly analysed?
quiz.explanation: Russell writes: 'what appears as Platonism is, when analysed, found to be in essence Pythagoreanism.'
quiz.related_concept: 'All things are numbers' and the mathematization of reality

quiz.prompt: The discovery of incommensurable magnitudes forced Greek mathematicians to develop ____ independently of arithmetic.
quiz.explanation: This separation, necessitated by incommensurables, culminates in Euclid's Elements.

quiz.prompt: Match each description to the correct term: (1) An impersonal natural law restoring balance among opposed elements; (2) The Pythagorean/Orphic doctrine that souls are reborn in new bodies; (3) Lengths sharing no common whole-number ratio.
quiz.explanation: Cosmic justice (Anaximander, Ch. II) restores elemental balance; transmigration is the Pythagorean/Orphic rebirth doctrine; incommensurables are magnitudes with no common whole-number ratio.
quiz.related_concept: Transmigration of souls and the Pythagorean religious order
